Day 1, tick 42 (8:30am): The rest of the I Corps comes up. Doubleday holds Robinson's division in reserve at the seminary, puts Rowley's division in line between Cutler and Meredith and toward the Millerstown road, and Buford's cavalry covers the flanks.

Day 3, tick 549 (12:00pm): Garnett's brigade of Pickett's division, with part of Armistead's, comes up to the stone wall at the Angle under canister and musketry; Webb's two regiments behind the wall, the 69th and 71st Pennsylvania, hold the front while the rest of the brigade stands behind the crest.

Day 2, tick 275 (9:05am): CHAMBERLAIN'S BAYONET CHARGE. Chamberlain reports that his line, with ammunition nearly gone and about to be overwhelmed, was ordered to the bayonet: "The word was enough." The regiment sweeps down the hill and the first Confederate line throws down its arms. Chamberlain reports 400 prisoners, mainly from the 15th and 47th Alabama with some of the 4th and 5th Texas, and 150 of the enemy killed and wounded in front of his position. // Contested: the hour of the charge (anywhere from about 5:10 to after 7 p.m. in different accounts); the figure of 400 is Chamberlain's own.

Day 2, tick 295 (10:45am): Crawford's Pennsylvania Reserves counterattack through the ground between Little Round Top and the Wheatfield and drive the Confederates back, taking many prisoners and the flag of a Georgia regiment. Colonel Charles F. Taylor of the 13th Pennsylvania Reserves (the Bucktails) is killed leading his regiment.

Day 3, tick 550 (12:05pm): GARNETT FALLS at the Angle. Lee's report counts him among the killed. Colonel Marshall, leading Pettigrew's brigade, also falls: Pettigrew's report lists him as wounded and taken prisoner, a letter of the same period as supposed killed. Pickett's three brigade commanders are all casualties.

Day 2, tick 328 (1:20pm): Avery is mortally wounded on the slope of Cemetery Hill and Colonel Godwin takes the brigade. // The note attributed to Avery ('Tell my father I died with my face to the enemy') comes from later accounts, not the Official Records.

Day 2, tick 242 (12:45pm): Law's brigade rejoins Hood about noon, and Longstreet then moves McLaws's and Hood's divisions toward the Confederate right. The route the engineers chose would have shown the column to the Union signal station, and the search for a more concealed road delays the march (Longstreet's report).

Day 2, tick 258 (7:40am): Hood is severely wounded soon after getting under fire and leaves the field; Law takes the division. Brigadier General G. T. Anderson is also severely wounded. // Hood's later claim that he asked to swing around Big Round Top is not in the Official Records.

Day 1, tick 95 (1:05pm): The Union line is taking shape on Cemetery Hill, Cemetery Ridge and toward Culp's Hill as reinforcements come up. By an order dated July 1 Meade puts Newton in command of the I Corps in place of Doubleday; Newton reports in person at the cemetery gate early on July 2.

Day 2, tick 254 (3:45pm): McLaws's division gets into position opposite the Union left about 4 p.m., and Hood's division is moved farther to the right, partly enveloping the Union left. Alexander's artillery battalion is posted to open on the Peach Orchard line.

Day 2, tick 273 (8:55am): An attack on the extreme right of Vincent's brigade forces back part of the 16th Michigan, which is broken and thrown into confusion; supported by the 140th New York, the line becomes firm again.

Day 2, tick 252 (7:10am): About 3 p.m. Meade rides to the left, finds Sickles's corps in advance of the line designed for it, and is explaining that it is too far forward and discussing withdrawing it when the Confederate batteries open and infantry columns come on in a vigorous assault.

Day 1, tick 56 (9:40am): Early's division arrives by the Heidlersburg road. Early opens with artillery on the columns moving against Doles's left and orders Gordon's brigade in on Doles's left; after an obstinate contest Gordon breaks Barlow's division and captures General Barlow, who is severely wounded. Doles's brigade attacks north of the town.

Day 3, tick 500 (8:05am): Pickett's three Virginia brigades (Garnett, Kemper, Armistead) form behind Seminary Ridge in the woods for the attack. Lee's report says they arrived near the field during the afternoon of July 2. // Contested: when Pickett's division reached the field (the afternoon of July 2 in Lee's report; about 9 a.m. July 3 in one timeline).

V-004 "The Railroad Cut" (tick 36): Lieutenant Colonel Rufus Dawes's 6th Wisconsin, with the 95th New York and the 14th Brooklyn, charged Davis's Confederates in the unfinished Railroad Cut north of the Chambersburg Pike. The men in the cut threw down their arms; the 6th Wisconsin sent to the rear 7 officers and about 225 men and took the 2nd Mississippi's flag.

V-009 "Vincent and Little Round Top" (tick 267): On July 2 Colonel Strong Vincent's brigade of the V Corps climbed Little Round Top and was posted on its southern slope, with the 20th Maine on the extreme left, minutes before the Confederate attack; Sykes's report says the troops were posted under Warren's direction. Vincent was mortally wounded in the fight and Colonel Rice took the brigade.

V-020 "Custer at East Cavalry Field" (tick 539): East of Gettysburg on the afternoon of July 3 Stuart's cavalry met Gregg's division and Custer's Michigan Brigade while the infantry assault was made at the center. Lee's report says the cavalry 'effectually protected our left' and that Hampton was seriously wounded. The hour of the main charges (about 3 p.m. by one account) and Custer's reported shout are from later accounts.

V-012 "The First Minnesota" (tick 302): With Confederate columns reaching the gap in the line on July 2, Hancock ordered Colonel Colvill's 1st Minnesota to take the enemy's colors, wanting to gain time until reinforcements came up. The regiment charged and drove the enemy back. Fox counts 262 engaged and 224 casualties, nearly all in this fight, none missing; 215 were killed or wounded on July 2 itself, the highest percentage of any Union regiment in a single battle in his tables.

V-013 "Greene's Lone Stand" (tick 315): When most of the XII Corps was sent to the left on July 2, Greene's brigade of five New York regiments (74 officers and 1,350 men by Geary's count, 1,424 in all) held the entrenched Culp's Hill alone against Johnson's division, which attacked about two hours after the opening on the right; Greene was reinforced during the evening by detachments from the I and XI Corps.

V-007 "Sickles Moves Forward" (tick 248): On July 2 Sickles's III Corps advanced from the line of Cemetery Ridge toward the Emmitsburg road, making a salient at the Peach Orchard. Meade's report says Sickles, 'not fully apprehending the instructions', was advancing half a mile to three-quarters of a mile in front of the Second Corps line when Meade found him about 3 p.m.; whether the move was authorized and when it began are disputed.

V-017 "The Cannonade" (tick 518): About 1 p.m. on July 3 the Confederate batteries opened together on the Union center and left at a given signal. Lee gives the hour as about 1 p.m.; Meade speaks of over 125 guns, Hunt of 100 to 120 bearing on the Union front, Pendleton of nearly 150 in position. The Union guns, about 80 in action by Hunt's count, withheld their fire through the first burst and then replied.

V-022 "Mudge and the Charge at Culp's Hill" (tick 483): On the morning of July 3 Colonel Colgrove sent the 2nd Massachusetts and the 27th Indiana across the open meadow in front of the Confederate breastworks on Culp's Hill. The 2nd Massachusetts lost about 130 killed and wounded, including its commander, Lieutenant Colonel Mudge, and the 27th Indiana 112. The hour is disputed and Mudge's reported last words come from survivors' later accounts.

Oak Ridge: Iverson's brigade attacked Baxter's brigade behind the stone wall here and lost heavily. Paul's brigade fought here; Paul and several of the colonels who succeeded him were wounded. Iverson's dead were buried on this ground. (elevation 600 ft)
Emmitsburg Road: Sickles advanced to this road July 2 creating his salient. Humphreys's division fought along it. Main Union approach route.
Big Round Top: Highest terrain on the battlefield. Fisher's brigade occupied it July 2 evening. Crawford's Pennsylvania Reserves advanced near its base. (elevation 785 ft)
Oak Hill: Confederate artillery on Oak Hill provided flanking fire on Union I Corps. Rodes's division attacked from here. (elevation 620 ft)
Benner's Hill: Latimer's Confederate battalion placed here July 2. Badly cut up by Union counter-battery fire. Major Joseph Latimer, aged 19, was mortally wounded. (elevation 610 ft)
Trostle Farm barn: Bigelow's withdrawal. A cannonball hole in the barn wall is shown today; its link to Bigelow's fight is tradition.
Copse of Trees: A clump of trees used as a reference point by the Confederate attackers during Pickett's Charge. The trees there now are later growth.
York Road: Smith's brigade of Early's division guarded the flank here on July 1; Early himself came by the Heidlersburg road.

Story marker "General Reynolds killed here about 10:15 AM July 1 (Doubleday; Howard gives 11:15) — directing the Iron Brigade into position" (tick 28)

Tour stop 1 "McPherson Ridge" (The Battle Begins — July 1, 7:30 AM; tick 12): On the morning of July 1, 1863, Union cavalry under Brigadier General John Buford deployed along McPherson's Ridge west of Gettysburg. When Heth's Confederate division advanced down the Chambersburg Pike, Buford's dismounted troopers fought a delaying action from behind fence rails and earthworks. Reynolds' I Corps then arrived. General John Reynolds rode forward to direct the Iron Brigade into Herbst Woods. Minutes later he was killed (a Confederate sharpshooter is the usual account; Heth believed a shell from Pegram's guns struck him) — one of the highest-ranking Union officers to die in the battle.

Tour stop 16 "Confederate Avenue" (The Retreat — July 4-5, 1863; tick 610): On the night of July 4-5, 1863, the Army of Northern Virginia began its retreat toward Virginia. A long wagon train of wounded men (Imboden's postwar account puts it at 17 miles) moved through driving rain toward the Potomac crossing at Williamsport. Meade did not pursue closely. President Lincoln was deeply disappointed that Lee's army escaped across the Potomac; in a letter to Meade that he did not send he wrote that Lee had been "within your easy grasp". Lee's army crossed the swollen Potomac on July 14, escaping to Virginia. The Gettysburg campaign was over. Estimated casualties: about 28,000 Confederate and about 23,000 Union (the Official Records return counts 20,451 and 23,049). Many
Story marker "Irish Brigade — Advanced into the Wheatfield; regimental tradition says the men wore sprigs of green boxwood in their caps" (tick 278)
Story marker "Hood wounded in the arm about 4:30 PM July 2 soon after the attack began (Lee's dispatch of July 4 says in the arm)" (tick 262)

Story marker "Hancock wounded here about 3:30 PM July 3 (Meade reports Hancock and Gibbon both severely wounded). His own dispatch says he was shot with a tenpenny nail and did not leave the field until the victory was secure" (tick 554)

Tour stop 2 "Oak Ridge" (The Union Right Flank — July 1, early afternoon; tick 52): At midday on July 1 Confederate forces under Rodes arrived on Oak Ridge north of the town, threatening the Union right flank. The XI Corps under Howard deployed north of Gettysburg to meet this threat. Iverson's North Carolina brigade attacked the stone wall held by Baxter's brigade of Robinson's division and was raked by musketry from behind it. Rodes wrote that its dead "lay in a distinctly marked line of battle", and many of its men, surrounded, were captured. Daniel's and Ramseur's brigades also attacked the Union line. By early afternoon the Union position north of town was becoming untenable.
Story marker "72nd PA — Webb's Philadelphia Brigade held The Angle against Pickett's Charge (the 72nd stood behind the crest; the 69th and 71st held the wall)" (tick 548)

Tour stop 11 "Cemetery Ridge" (Wright's Breakthrough — July 2, 7:30 PM; tick 315): In the fading light of July 2, Ambrose Wright's Georgia brigade was, in Lee's report, the brigade that gained the crest of the ridge itself. Lee reports that Wright, having become separated from McLaws and gone beyond the other brigades of his division, was attacked in front and on both flanks and compelled to retire, unable to bring off any of the captured artillery. The crisis passed. Whether the fight shaped Lee's decision to attack the center the next day is a matter of interpretation.

Tour stop 13 "East Cavalry Field" (Stuart vs. Custer — July 3, 3:00 PM; tick 539): While Pickett's Charge unfolded a mile to the west, Stuart's cavalry fought Gregg's Union cavalry division and Custer's Michigan brigade east of the town. Pleasonton's report says a heavy force of cavalry attempted to gain the Union rear and was defeated by Gregg, with several fine charges by the 1st Michigan Cavalry (OR 27/1 p.916). Lee's report says the cavalry effectually protected the Confederate left and that Hampton was seriously wounded. Custer is reported to have led a Michigan regiment against Hampton's brigade at a gallop, shouting "Come on, you Wolverines!" — a report from veterans' later accounts.
